content.content: zio m (plural zii, feminine zia, augmentative (uncommon) zióne, diminutive-endearing ziétto or (less common) ziìno or ziùccio)
Inherited from Late Latin thius, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Spanish tío, Portuguese tio, Sicilian ziu, Sardinian tiu or tziu, Venetan sio.
gatto m (plural gatti, feminine gatta, diminutive gattìno, augmentative gattóne, pejorative gattàccio or gattonàccio, derogatory gattùccio)

From sedere.
The initial auto-gemination found in some regional Italian varieties seems to be unetymological.
albero m (plural alberi, diminutive alberèllo or alberétto or alberìno, augmentative alberóne, pejorative alberàccio, derogatory alberùccio)
From older alboro m (via dissimilation), from albore m (via masculinization of the ending), from Latin arborem f.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *albarus, a derivative of Latin albus (“white”).
acqua f (plural acque, diminutive acquerèlla or acquétta or acquicèlla or acquolìna)

content: stretch or expanse of water; body of water

content.content: artista m or f by sense (masculine plural artisti, feminine plural artiste)

From Latin diurnālis (with influence from giorno (“day”)), from Latin diurnus, from Latin diēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Originally an adjective meaning "daily" (modern giornaliero) as a modifier for foglio giornale.
giornale m or f by sense (plural giornali)

From Latin diurnālis (with influence from giorno (“day”)), from Latin diurnus, from Latin diēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Originally an adjective meaning "daily" (modern giornaliero) as a modifier for foglio giornale.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(il)lu, from Latin illum, illud, by dropping il- and -m. Cognate with Sicilian lu.
